headline: High-for-longer inflation, record government debt, AI spending boom and defence build-up are structural tailwinds for the next 5-10 years
reasoning: O'Connor outlined four structural macro themes he sees persisting for 5-10 years: higher-for-longer inflation and therefore higher interest rates; record government debt as governments cannot stop spending (the US borrowing more, Australia taxing more); record spending on AI reverberating through many sectors; and record spending on defence and security due to a fractured geopolitical environment. He views these as the foundational backdrop informing how Regal has structured its portfolio.
quote: The foundations around the investment landscape that we think we're investing in, that we think we've got products to respond to are still ever present. And we think of that as high for longer inflation and therefore higher interest rates record government debt because the governments can't stop spending. And therefore in the US they're solving that by borrowing more in Australia. As you can see, we're simply taxing the taxpayers more. That creates a erosion of confidence in the government and their promises, particularly around government debt. You've got record spending on AI that is reverberating through many sectors of the economy. And the fourth thing I'd say is you've got a record amount going into defence and security more generally because of fractured geopolitical environment. We see that's the backdrop to investing. That won't go away for the next 5 to 10 years, and that informs how we have structured our investments to better position for that environment.

headline: Cautiously optimistic on S&P 500 but urging reduced risk appetite, diversification, income, and downside protection as AI-driven earnings growth becomes increasingly narrow
reasoning: O'Connor draws on internal views from Regal's portfolio managers including Paul Moore, Phil King, and Adrian Redlich, noting that while US corporate earnings growth is at its highest outside of post-recession rebounds, the growth is increasingly concentrated around AI expenditure. He draws on historical precedent around large concentrated expenditure themes to advise caution. He suggests dialling back risk appetite from an eight out of ten to something lower, seeking diversification, income-producing assets, inflation protection and downside protection. He is not predicting an imminent bubble burst but believes this is not the time to load up on the S&P 500 indiscriminately.
quote: The collective view in house is actually that the world is in a delicate position at the moment. Whilst we have the highest increase in earnings in American companies outside of a rebound from some sort of economic event, and that paints a very, very good picture that economic growth is increasingly becoming very narrow around this AI expenditure, thematic. And so that causes. And history will tell you this cause for caution. So we're not saying that it's about to end or that there's a bubble that's about to burst, but we certainly are utilizing our memory from previous big expenditures like this to say there's probably a time for caution, in your view, of risk appetite was, let's say, at eight out of ten, 18 months ago, you might want to dial it back a tad from that and therefore seek diversification, seek assets that are producing income, have some inflation protection and better still, some downside protection.

headline: Smooth leadership transition underway as Phil King retires by June 2027, with business processes and investment management already separated to ensure continuity

headline: Counter-drone detection and defeat business benefiting from US Safer Skies Act regulatory changes, expanding addressable market to 17,500 local and state law enforcement agencies
reasoning: The speaker outlines that regulatory changes, particularly the US Safer Skies Act, have opened up the counter-drone market beyond federal/military use to local and state law enforcement agencies, significantly expanding the addressable market. The business operates in two areas: detecting drones and defeating/countering them. The company is investing heavily in R&D — $40 million in H1 alone, $70 million the prior year — to stay ahead of evolving drone technology. New next-generation products including AI-powered detection software (RFA Buy Three) and new hardware (RF Recon) were released in July-August, representing a four-year development effort. The speaker sees drone and counter-drone as industries that are not going away, driven by both military restocking dynamics and civilian/infrastructure protection needs.
quote: The changes in regulation are helping, particularly, for example, in the US market. They've recently changed a thing called the Safer Skies Act. The Safer Skies Act has opened up a counter drone, which is what we focus on, are to local and law enforcement agencies. So previously Counter Drone was kept for military and army purposes and federal purposes. And now 17,500 local and state law enforcement agencies across the US can use counter drone. So there's a situation where regulatory changes have actually helped our business. And we're seeing similar discussions in Australia and the United Kingdom.
